HTTP is defined as a stateless protocol, meaning that each request message's semantics can be understood in isolation, and that the relationship between connections and messages on them has no impact on the interpretation of those messages.
For example, a CONNECT request (Section 9.3.6) or a request with the Upgrade header field (Section 7.8) can occur at any time, not just in the first message on a connection.
Many implementations depend on HTTP's stateless design in order to reuse proxied connections or dynamically load balance requests across multiple servers.
As a result, a server assume that two requests on the same connection are from the same user agent unless the connection is secured and specific to that agent.
Some non-standard HTTP extensions (e.g., ) have been known to violate this requirement, resulting in security and interoperability problems.

pages.title: HTTP Methods Explained: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE & More
passages: # HTTP Methods Explained: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE & More
API Design19 min read
## The Myth: HTTP Methods Are Just Labels
Why bother with DELETE?
The reality: HTTP methods have precise semantic contracts defined in **RFC 9110** (published June 2022, the current HTTP semantics standard that supersedes RFC 7231).
Those contracts carry real consequences.
A `GET` response can be cached by a CDN, a proxy, or the browser, transparently, without your involvement.
A `PUT` request can be retried automatically by an HTTP client after a timeout without creating duplicate records.
A `POST` cannot be retried safely.
## Key Takeaways
* ▸**Safe methods** (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) are guaranteed read-only. Caches, crawlers, and prefetch systems call them freely.
* ▸**Idempotent methods** (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, TRACE) can be retried safely after a network timeout. POST cannot.
The current authoritative references are:
* **RFC 9110** (June 2022), "HTTP Semantics." Defines GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, and TRACE. Supersedes RFC 7231.
* **RFC 5789** (March 2010), Defines the PATCH method, which was intentionally omitted from the original HTTP/1.1 spec.
RFC 9110 also defines three critical properties that every method either has or lacks, and these properties drive the behavior of every HTTP intermediary in the path between client and server.
## Safe, Idempotent, and Cacheable: Precise Definitions
A method is **safe**if the client's intended semantics are read-only.
The server may still perform side effects (logging, analytics updates), but those are incidental to the request, not caused by the client.
Safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE.
The practical consequences of safety: web crawlers, link prefetchers, and browser "hover to prefetch" features call safe methods freely.
A method is **idempotent** if the intended effect on the server is the same whether the request is sent once or ten times.
Idempotent methods: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, TRACE.
POST is not idempotent.
Important nuance: idempotent does not mean "returns the same response code every time." `DELETE /users/123` returns 200 the first call (resource deleted) and 404 the second (resource already gone).
Both are correct, the state of the server (user 123 does not exist) is the same after either call.
The practical consequence: HTTP clients can automatically retry idempotent requests after a network timeout.
PUT and DELETE are not cacheable.
| Method | RFC | Safe | Idempotent | Cacheable | Has Request Body |
| HEAD | RFC 9110 §9.3.2 | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| TRACE | RFC 9110 §9.3.8 | Yes | Yes | No | No |
## Each HTTP Method in Depth
The resource defines what that means, it can create a new subordinate resource (most common), process a form, append to a log, trigger an action, or anything else.
POST is neither safe nor idempotent: two identical POST requests may create two separate resources.

# Manual OPTIONS, what methods does this endpoint support? OPTIONS /users/123 HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com HTTP/1.1 200 OK Allow: GET, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS Accept-Patch: application/merge-patch+json, application/json-patch+json # CORS preflight, browser sends this automatically before cross-origin requests OPTIONS /api/orders HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Origin: https://app.example.com Access-Control-Request-Method: POST Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type HTTP/1.1 204 No Content Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400 # Cache this preflight response for 24h
### CONNECT: Tunnel Establishment
CONNECT requests a proxy to establish a TCP tunnel to the destination server.

It is used by browsers when connecting to HTTPS sites through an HTTP proxy. `CONNECT api.example.com:443` tells the proxy to open a raw TCP connection to port 443; the browser then performs its TLS handshake through that tunnel.
Application developers rarely implement CONNECT directly.
### TRACE: Diagnostic Loop-Back
TRACE performs a message loop-back diagnostic.
The server echoes the request back as the response body, letting clients see what intermediaries (proxies, gateways) modified in transit.
TRACE is disabled in all modern browsers due to the **Cross-Site Tracing (XST) attack**, it can expose cookies and authentication headers to JavaScript via XMLHttpRequest.
Web servers should disable TRACE in production.

// WRONG: Only implement POST handler, forget OPTIONS app.post('/api/orders', createOrder); // Browser sends OPTIONS preflight → 404 or 405 → CORS error → POST never fires // RIGHT: Handle OPTIONS explicitly (or use a middleware) // Express.js app.options('/api/orders', cors(corsOptions)); app.post('/api/orders', cors(corsOptions), createOrder); // OR use cors() middleware globally before routes app.use(cors({ origin: 'https://app.example.com', methods: ['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'], allowedHeaders: ['Authorization', 'Content-Type'], maxAge: 86400, // cache preflight 24h, reduces OPTIONS request volume })); // FastAPI (Python), OPTIONS is handled automatically with CORSMiddleware from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware app.add_middleware(CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=["https://app.example.com"], ...)
An idempotent method produces the same server state whether called once or ten times.
GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, and TRACE are idempotent.
POST is not, calling POST /orders twice creates two orders.
DELETE.
It is idempotent, DELETE /users/123 called twice is safe: the first returns 200 or 204, the second 404.
Never use GET /users/123/delete, as web crawlers and prefetch mechanisms will trigger it.
Never return 200 with an empty body from a resource-creating POST.
### What is the HEAD method used for?
HEAD is identical to GET but the server must not return a response body.

A header consists of lines of [ASCII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASCII "ASCII")[text](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plain_text "Plain text"); each terminated with a [carriage return](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carriage_return "Carriage return") and [line feed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_feed "Line feed") sequence.

The HTTP/1.0 specification[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc1945-3):§8 defined the GET, HEAD, and POST methods as well as listing the PUT, DELETE, LINK and UNLINK methods under additional methods.
However, the HTTP/1.1 specification[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc2616-36):§9 added five new methods: PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, and TRACE.
Any client can use any method and the server can be configured to support any combination of methods.
A request method is _safe_ if a request with that method has no intended effect on the server.
The methods GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, and QUERY are defined as safe.
In other words, safe methods are intended to be [read-only](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command%E2%80%93query_separation "Command–query separation").
In contrast, the methods POST, PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, and PATCH are not safe.
The methods GET, HEAD, and POST are defined as cacheable.
In contrast, the methods PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, TRACE, and PATCH are not cacheable.
### Response
Since 1992, a new document was written to specify the evolution of the basic protocol towards its next full version.
It supported both the simple request method of the 0.9 version and the full GET request that included the client HTTP version.
This was the first of the many unofficial HTTP/1.0 drafts that preceded the final work on HTTP/1.0.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-Tim_Berner-Lee-1992-45)
End-user adoption of the new versions of browsers and servers was rapid.
In 2020, the first drafts of HTTP/3 were published and major web browsers and web servers started to adopt it.
On 6 June 2022, IETF standardized HTTP/3 as RFC[9114](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc9114-69).
### Updates and refactoring in 2022
In June 2022, RFC documents were published that deprecated many of the previous documents and introducing a few minor changes and a refactoring of HTTP semantics description into a separate document.
* RFC[9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)–"HTTP Semantics,"[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc9110-19)_Internet Standard 97._

passages: # HTTP/1.1 Explained: RFC 9110 and RFC 9112 Messages, Methods and Security
| method | request line | GET, POST, PUT and so on | Case sensitive token. A server that sees a method longer than any it implements should answer 501 |

| request-target | request line | Path and query, or a full URI, or host:port, or `*` | Four forms: origin-form, absolute-form (to proxies), authority-form (CONNECT), asterisk-form (server wide OPTIONS). No whitespace allowed |
| HTTP-version | both start lines | `HTTP/1.1` | Case sensitive. Intermediaries must send their own version, not forward the client's blindly |
| absolute-form | `http://www.example.org/where?q=now` | Requests to a forward proxy |
| authority-form | `www.example.org:443` | CONNECT only, to open a tunnel |
| asterisk-form | `*` | Server wide OPTIONS |
1. A response to HEAD, and any 1xx, 204 or 304 response, ends at the empty line. No body, no matter what the fields say.
2. A 2xx response to CONNECT turns the connection into a tunnel right after the header section.

3. If both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length are present, Transfer-Encoding wins. The RFC adds that such a message "might indicate an attempt to perform request smuggling" and "ought to be handled as an error". An intermediary that forwards it must strip Content-Length first.
### Methods
RFC 9110 section 9 defines eight methods and classifies each as safe (read only in intent) and idempotent (repeating it has the same intended effect as sending it once):
| Method | Purpose | Safe | Idempotent |
| DELETE | Remove all current representations | no | yes |
| CONNECT | Establish a tunnel to the server named by the target | no | no |
| OPTIONS | Describe the communication options for the target | yes | yes |
| TRACE | Message loop back test along the path | yes | yes |
These properties are not trivia.
RFC 9110 explains that idempotent requests "can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs", and that a proxy "MUST NOT automatically retry non-idempotent requests".

TRACE reflects the received request back to the client, and RFC 9110 warns that a client must not put sensitive data in a TRACE request and that the final recipient should strip fields likely to carry it.
### Status codes
### Persistent connections
HTTP/1.0 opened a new TCP connection for every request unless both sides used the nonstandard `Keep-Alive` mechanism.
HTTP/1.1 reversed the default.
A client on a persistent connection may pipeline, which means sending several requests without waiting for each response.
RFC 9112 section 9.3.2 lets a server process pipelined requests with safe methods in parallel, but it "MUST send the corresponding responses in the same order that the requests were received".
Responses carry no identifier tying them to requests; order is the only link.
| HTTP/0.9 | Before HTTP/1.0, no RFC | Request line only, no header fields, so no name based virtual hosting (RFC 9112 Appendix C.1) |
| HTTP/1.0, RFC 1945 | May 1996 | Header fields in requests and responses; a new connection per request unless both sides used the nonstandard Keep-Alive |
| HTTP/1.1, RFC 2068 | January 1997 | First Standards Track HTTP/1.1: Host, chunked coding, persistent connections by default, caching controls |
The design allows this because of several historical tolerances:

* **Two length signals.** Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding can both appear. RFC 9112 explains that early implementations sent both, a chunked body plus an estimated length "for use by progress bars", which is why the standard made Transfer-Encoding override Content-Length rather than forbidding the combination. Any hop that does not follow that rule exactly, or that only speaks HTTP/1.0, can disagree with the others.

* **Lenient whitespace and line endings.** RFC 9112 lets recipients treat a bare LF as a line ending and lets them parse request lines on any whitespace. It immediately warns that "lenient parsing can result in request smuggling security vulnerabilities if there are multiple recipients of the message and each has its own unique interpretation of robustness".
RFC 9110 section 17.5 notes that because HTTP uses "mostly textual, character-delimited fields", parsers are often vulnerable to "very long (or very slow) streams of data".

The standard sets minimum sizes that implementations should support but leaves the maximums to operators, and warns that failing to limit method names, field names, numeric values and chunk lengths "can result in arbitrary code execution due to buffer or arithmetic overflows".
That is why server limits on header size, header count, body size and read timeouts are security settings, not just tuning.
In the `-v` output, look for `Strict-Transport-Security`, `Set-Cookie` attributes, `Cache-Control` on pages that set cookies, and a `Server` value that does not advertise a version.
To confirm TRACE is disabled on your own server, the curl manual's `-X, --request` option sets a custom method:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X TRACE https://your-site.example/
A 405 means TRACE is refused.
Note the curl manual's own warning that `-X` passes the method string "verbatim" without filtering, so use it only for a deliberate check like this one.
Then confirm what nginx actually loaded.
The nginx command line documentation describes `-t` as testing the configuration and `-T` as the same "but additionally dump configuration files to standard output":

pages.title: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics | RFC Editor
passages: * J. Reschke, Ed.
Internet Standard
## [Copyright Notice](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-copyright-notice)
Copyright (c) 2022 IETF Trust and the persons identified as the document authors.
All rights reserved.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-boilerplate.2-1)

The client examines received responses to see if its intentions were carried out, determining what to do next based on the status codes and content received.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.3-2)

HTTP semantics include the intentions defined by each request method ([Section 9](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#methods)), extensions to those semantics that might be described in request header fields, status codes that describe the response ([Section 15](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#status.codes)), and other control data and resource metadata that might be given in response fields.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.3-3)

Semantics also include representation metadata that describe how content is intended to be interpreted by a recipient, request header fields that might influence content selection, and the various selection algorithms that are collectively referred to as "content negotiation" ([Section 12](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#content.negotiation)).[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.3-4)

This specification uses the Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF) notation of [[RFC5234](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#RFC5234)], extended with the notation for case-sensitivity in strings defined in [[RFC7405](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#RFC7405)].[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.1-1)

It also uses a list extension, defined in [Section 5.6.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#abnf.extension), that allows for compact definition of comma-separated lists using a "#" operator (similar to how the "*" operator indicates repetition). [Appendix A](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#collected.abnf) shows the collected grammar with all list operators expanded to standard ABNF notation.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.1-2)
As a convention, ABNF rule names prefixed with "obs-" denote obsolete grammar rules that appear for historical reasons.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.1-3)
## [3.](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3)[Terminology and Core Concepts](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-terminology-and-core-concep)
HTTP was created for the World Wide Web (WWW) architecture and has evolved over time to support the scalability needs of a worldwide hypertext system.
Much of that architecture is reflected in the terminology used to define HTTP.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3-1)

One design goal of HTTP is to separate resource identification from request semantics, which is made possible by vesting the request semantics in the request method ([Section 9](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#methods)) and a few request-modifying header fields.
A resource cannot treat a request in a manner inconsistent with the semantics of the method of the request.

For example, though the URI of a resource might imply semantics that are not safe, a client can expect the resource to avoid actions that are unsafe when processing a request with a safe method (see [Section 9.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#safe.methods)).[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.1-2)

HTTP relies upon the Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) standard [[URI](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#URI)] to indicate the target resource ([Section 7.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#target.resource)) and relationships between resources.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.1-3)

HTTP is defined as a stateless protocol, meaning that each request message's semantics can be understood in isolation, and that the relationship between connections and messages on them has no impact on the interpretation of those messages.

For example, a CONNECT request ([Section 9.3.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#CONNECT)) or a request with the Upgrade header field ([Section 7.8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#field.upgrade)) can occur at any time, not just in the first message on a connection.

Many implementations depend on HTTP's stateless design in order to reuse proxied connections or dynamically load balance requests across multiple servers.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.3-4)
As a result, a server MUST NOT assume that two requests on the same connection are from the same user agent unless the connection is secured and specific to that agent.

Some non-standard HTTP extensions (e.g., [[RFC4559](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#RFC4559)]) have been known to violate this requirement, resulting in security and interoperability problems.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.3-5)
### [3.4.](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.4)[Messages](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-messages)
request >

Field values containing CR, LF, or NUL characters are invalid and dangerous, due to the varying ways that implementations might parse and interpret those characters; a recipient of CR, LF, or NUL within a field value MUST either reject the message or replace each of those characters with SP before further processing or forwarding of that message.

Field values containing other CTL characters are also invalid; however, recipients MAY retain such characters for the sake of robustness when they appear within a safe context (e.g., an application-specific quoted string that will not be processed by any downstream HTTP parser).[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-5.5-5)
Fields that only anticipate a single member as the field value are referred to as "singleton fields".[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-5.5-6)

pages.title: RFC 9110 Explained: Safe & Idempotent HTTP Methods
passages: # RFC 9110 Explained: Safe & Idempotent HTTP Methods
A practical guide to safe, idempotent, and cacheable HTTP methods, with examples and links to the official RFC 9110 sections.
3. [Method Properties at a Glance](#properties)
4. [Safe Methods (Section 9.2.1)](#safe)
5. [Idempotent Methods (Section 9.2.2)](#idempotent)
[RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110) is the IETF standard that defines HTTP semantics.
The IETF published it in June 2022 as Internet Standard STD 97.
Roy Fielding, Mark Nottingham, and Julian Reschke edited it.
For the normative text, see [the official RFC 9110 specification](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110).
A safe method does not request a state change.
An idempotent method has the same intended effect when a client repeats an identical request.
For REST API work, three parts of RFC 9110 matter most.
Section 9.2 classifies methods as safe, idempotent, or cacheable.
Section 9.3 defines each method.
## What Is a Target Resource in RFC 9110?
A resource is the thing an HTTP request addresses.
A target URI identifies that resource.
One resource can have different representations.

[Section 3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-3.1) defines resources. [Section 3.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-3.2) explains representations. [Section 7.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-7.1) explains how a request identifies its target URI.
This table records what RFC 9110 states for each method it defines.
PATCH is included for comparison, but a separate standard defines it.
| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Cacheable | Section |
| **DELETE** | No | Yes | No | 9.3.5 |
| **CONNECT** | No | No | No | 9.3.6 |
| **OPTIONS** | Yes | Yes | No | 9.3.7 |
| **TRACE** | Yes | Yes | No | 9.3.8 |
| **PATCH**\* | No | No | No | RFC 5789 |
\*RFC 5789 defines PATCH, not RFC 9110.
A server can make PATCH idempotent by design, but the standard does not require it.
## Safe Methods (Section 9.2.1)
The client does not request a state change on the origin server, and does not expect one.
[Section 9.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-9.2.1) defines four safe methods: **GET**, **HEAD**, **OPTIONS**, and **TRACE**.
The distinction exists so that crawlers and pre-fetch caches can act without harm to the server.
Note the limit of the guarantee.
A method is idempotent when the intended effect of two or more identical requests is the same as the effect of one request.
[Section 9.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-9.2.2) states that **PUT**, **DELETE**, and the safe request methods are idempotent.
The safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE.
The complete idempotent set is therefore **GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, and DELETE**. **POST** and **CONNECT** are not idempotent.

# Idempotent: the resource holds the same value after one request or ten PUT /users/123 { "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" } # Idempotent: after the first request the resource is gone and stays gone DELETE /users/123 # NOT idempotent: each request creates another user POST /users { "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" }
A retried POST creates a duplicate, so POST needs an [idempotency key](/idempotency) to become safe to retry.
As with safe methods, the guarantee covers the intended effect only.
A server can log each request separately or keep a revision history for every idempotent request.
* **POST** — cacheable only with explicit freshness information and a `Content-Location` header field equal to the target URI
* **PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, TRACE** — responses are not cacheable
A cached POST response can satisfy a later GET or HEAD request for the same URI.
| 9.3.5 | DELETE | Remove the association between the target and its function |
| 9.3.6 | CONNECT | Establish a tunnel to the origin server |
| 9.3.7 | OPTIONS | Request the communication options for a resource |
| 9.3.8 | TRACE | Request a loop-back of the request message |
Our [HTTP methods guide](/http-methods) covers each of these with request and response examples.
The [OPTIONS deep dive](/http-methods-options) covers CORS preflight in detail.
## Why PATCH Is Not Here
This causes a common error.
Developers look for PATCH in Section 9.3, do not find it, and conclude that PATCH is non-standard.
PATCH is standard.
A server can design an idempotent PATCH.
Our [PATCH deep dive](/http-methods-patch) shows how, and covers JSON Patch and JSON Merge Patch.
## What RFC 9110 Replaced
| 9.2 | Common method properties | [Idempotency](/idempotency) |
| 9.3 | Method definitions | [HTTP methods](/http-methods) |
| 10 | Message context header fields | [HTTP headers](/http-headers) |
## Frequently Asked Questions
### Which HTTP methods are idempotent in RFC 9110?
Section 9.2.2 states that PUT, DELETE, and the safe request methods are idempotent.
The safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE.
The full idempotent set is therefore GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, and DELETE.
POST and CONNECT are not idempotent.
### Which HTTP methods are safe in RFC 9110?
Section 9.2.1 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE as safe.
A safe method is read-only in its defined semantics.
Every safe method is also idempotent.
### Which HTTP methods are cacheable in RFC 9110?
Responses to GET and HEAD are cacheable.
Responses to PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, and TRACE are not.
A POST response is cacheable only with explicit freshness information and a `Content-Location` header field equal to the target URI.
No.
RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, and TRACE in Section 9.3.
RFC 5789 defines PATCH separately.
Cite RFC 9110.
It obsoleted RFC 7231 in June 2022.
The semantics did not change, but RFC 7231 is no longer the current reference.
